strengths: ArtVIP addresses a meaningful robotics infrastructure need with 992 articulated assets, 3,965 joints, six scenes, standardized part annotations, and embedded interaction behaviors on 394 assets. The combination could provide substantial practical value.

The real-robot imitation-learning experiments provide encouraging evidence of usefulness. Adding simulated demonstrations improves ACT and Diffusion Policy across four tasks, and the unseen-microwave comparison favors ArtVIP over PartNet-Mobility under matched demonstration counts.

Optical motion tracking provides direct physical validation beyond visual inspection. The drawer experiments test four applied forces, and additional microwave and oven experiments examine triggered mechanisms.
The appendix supplies useful category statistics, authoring-time estimates, training hyperparameters, per-seed imitation-learning results, and runtime profiling.
weaknesses: The central physics formulation contains substantive errors. Equation 3c defines friction as -D*qdot*sign(qdot), which is negative for either velocity direction and therefore reinforces motion when velocity is negative. Equation 3 also adds force and torque magnitudes without a dimensional conversion. Equations 1–2 use positive position and velocity errors for the applied drive, requiring an unexplained sign convention to produce restoring forces. These issues leave unclear whether the implemented dynamics match the stated method.

The claimed RL sim-to-real correlation is unsupported by the reported data. Section 5.3 and Appendix K claim r=0.9886 from Table 3, but that table compares EAGLE with vision-based PPO rather than simulation with real-world performance. The correlation between its two reported rows is approximately 0.946, and the actual paired simulation/real-world success rates are absent. This prevents verification of a central fidelity claim.

Physical validation is too narrow to establish fidelity across the collection. The presented evidence covers a drawer, microwave, and oven, without aggregate trajectory-error metrics, uncertainty bands, or a clearly separated calibration/test protocol. The parameter-fitting procedure and measurement of mass, inertia, friction, and damping across the remaining assets are insufficiently specified.

The downstream evaluation does not isolate the proposed improvements. The four digital-twin tasks lack alternative-asset baselines, while the matched PartNet-Mobility comparison covers only one task and one unseen real microwave. There are no controlled ablations separating appearance, collision geometry, tuned dynamics, and modular behaviors, nor a downstream comparison with BEHAVIOR-1K. Consequently, the results establish utility more convincingly than the claimed causes of improved transfer.

Visual-realism evidence is largely qualitative. Triangle counts measure geometric complexity rather than accuracy, t-SNE plots of CLIP features do not quantify photorealism or distribution alignment, and the VGGT comparison lacks aggregate reconstruction metrics. Appendix L compares reconstruction on two real objects against published synthetic-data results, which does not constitute a controlled comparison demonstrating ArtVIP's superiority.

Several dataset claims exceed the documented evidence. The annotation vocabulary primarily describes semantic parts rather than explicit action affordances. Simulator-independent reuse of embedded behaviors is not demonstrated through USD-to-URDF/MJCF conversion. Broad claims that competing datasets lack modular interaction, or that comparable interactive scenes are unique to ArtVIP, require more careful positioning and feature-level evidence.

strengths: ArtVIP addresses a meaningful robotics infrastructure need with 992 articulated assets, 3,965 joints, six scenes, standardized modeling conventions, and part annotations. Embedded interaction behaviors across 394 assets could provide substantial practical value.

Real-world experiments provide encouraging evidence of utility: adding simulated demonstrations improves ACT and Diffusion Policy across four tasks, and the microwave comparison favors ArtVIP over PartNet-Mobility under matched demonstration counts.

The appendices provide useful category statistics, estimated production effort, simulation throughput, training hyperparameters, per-seed imitation-learning results, and additional motion-capture comparisons.
weaknesses: The physical-fidelity formulation contains substantive errors. In Appendix E, Eq. 3c gives friction as −D·q_dot·sign(q_dot), which always points in the negative direction and therefore assists negative motion instead of opposing it. The static-friction threshold also adds force and torque magnitudes without explaining dimensional conversion. Whether these are documentation errors or implemented behavior must be resolved.

The claimed RL sim-to-real correlation is unsupported by the reported data. Section 5.3 and Appendix K cite Table 3 for r = 0.9886, but that table compares EAGLE with vision-based PPO, rather than simulation with real-world success rates. The paired measurements needed to verify this central claim are absent.

Physical validation is too narrow to establish fidelity across the collection. The drawer, microwave, and oven examples show selected trajectory agreement, but there are no aggregate error metrics, clearly separated calibration and held-out evaluation conditions, or representative coverage of the thousands of joints. The parameter-fitting procedure and its validation remain insufficiently specified.

Visual realism is assessed mainly through triangle counts, qualitative reconstruction examples, and a CLIP t-SNE plot. More triangles do not establish geometric accuracy, and t-SNE overlap does not quantify photorealism. Comparisons using semantically similar objects also confound asset quality with object identity. Controlled quantitative measurements are needed.

Downstream experiments do not isolate the proposed sources of improvement. Mixed-data experiments increase the total demonstration count, and no ablations separately test textures, geometry, joint tuning, or modular behaviors. The direct dataset comparison covers only one task and one unseen real microwave, with no comparable BEHAVIOR-1K policy evaluation. This supports limited utility rather than broad superiority.

Reproducibility and portability are incompletely substantiated. The supplied manuscript leaves the dataset availability link blank, does not specify a license or sufficiently concrete behavior implementation, and provides no demonstration that embedded interactions survive conversion to URDF or MJCF. These omissions matter particularly because the primary contribution is a reusable dataset.

strengths: ArtVIP addresses a meaningful robotics infrastructure need with 992 articulated assets, six scenes, consistent modeling standards, part annotations, and embedded interaction behaviors. The collection could substantially reduce simulation setup effort.

Real-robot experiments provide encouraging evidence of utility. Adding simulated demonstrations improves ACT and Diffusion Policy across four tasks; the unseen-microwave comparison also favors ArtVIP over PartNet-Mobility under matched demonstration counts.
Physical validation goes beyond visual inspection: motion capture compares real and simulated drawer, microwave, and oven behavior, including multiple applied forces for the drawer.
The appendices provide useful implementation details, modeling-time estimates, runtime profiling, training hyperparameters, and per-seed imitation-learning results.
weaknesses: The RL sim-to-real claim has a major reporting inconsistency. Section 5.3 and Appendix K attribute a simulation-versus-real correlation of 0.9886 to Table 3, but that table reports EAGLE versus vision-based PPO, with no paired simulation and real-world success rates. Consequently, the claimed real-world RL transfer and correlation cannot be verified.

The physical formulation contains substantive errors as written. Equation 3c gives friction as −D·q̇·sign(q̇), which is negative for either velocity direction and therefore assists motion when q̇ is negative. The static-friction threshold also adds force and torque magnitudes without explaining a dimensionally consistent conversion. These issues require correction and clarification of what the implementation actually executes.

Collection-wide physical-fidelity claims substantially exceed the validation. Only a few objects are examined, without aggregate trajectory-error metrics, uncertainty bands, or a clear separation between calibration and held-out evaluation conditions. The procedure for identifying and validating physical parameters across all 992 assets is insufficiently specified.

Visual realism is supported mainly by selected renderings, triangle counts, qualitative VGGT reconstructions, and a CLIP t-SNE plot. Triangle count does not establish geometric accuracy, and t-SNE proximity does not quantify photorealism. Comparisons using corresponding versus merely semantically similar objects introduce additional confounds. Controlled quantitative appearance and geometry evaluations are needed.

The downstream evaluation does not adequately isolate the proposed advantages. The four primary tasks compare 100 real demonstrations against larger mixed datasets without alternative-asset controls. The matched PartNet-Mobility comparison is valuable but covers only one task and one real target, with no reported uncertainty. Ablations separating appearance, collision geometry, calibrated dynamics, and embedded behaviors are missing.

Several resource and positioning claims remain insufficiently demonstrated. Behavior portability beyond Isaac Sim is not tested, and USD-to-URDF/MJCF conversion alone does not establish preservation of embedded interactions. Broad claims about competing platforms and dataset uniqueness are weakly supported. Overall, the promising collection and positive imitation-learning results do not yet outweigh the unresolved soundness and evaluation issues.
